claims.claim: A/A simulation, 1,000 runs, 200 users per arm per look, rate 10%: 5.2% false positives with 1 look, 12.9% with 5, 18.4% with 10.
claims.source: Simulated with NumPy 2.4.6 in this repository (seed 1).

concept_html:
A test's 5% false positive rate holds only if you analyse once, at the planned sample size. Common habits break it.

Peeking. Checking results every day and stopping the first time p < 0.05 gives the noise ten chances to cross the line. A simulation in this course's build: two identical arms with a 10% conversion rate, 1,000 runs, 200 users per arm per look. One look: 5.2% false positives. Five looks: 12.9%. Ten looks: 18.4%.

Fixes, in order of simplicity:

  • Fixed horizon. Compute the sample size (lesson B9-L1), run to it, analyse once. Dashboards during the test show health metrics and the split check, not the lift.
  • Planned interim looks with a group-sequential design, where each look uses a stricter threshold so the overall rate stays at 5%. Plan the number of looks and the boundaries before launch.
  • Always-valid methods designed for continuous monitoring,, offered by some experimentation platforms. Use them as the platform documents them.

Novelty and learning effects. Users click a new button because it is new. The lift fades after a week. Run for at least one full weekly cycle, and compare the effect in week 1 and week 2.

Too many metrics. Twenty secondary metrics produce about one false positive per test (lesson B8-L3). Name one primary metric and a few guardrails before launch.

Stopping for a good result only. A team that stops early when B looks good but runs longer when B looks bad biases every conclusion towards B.

Interference. If treated users affect control users, through shared inventory, pricing or social features, the arms are not independent. Randomise at a level that contains the interaction, such as city or store.

Write the plan down: primary metric, MDE, sample size, duration, looks, and the decision rule. Then follow it.

lines: from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TestPlan:
"""Written before launch and stored with the results."""
primary_metric: str
mde_points: float
n_per_arm: int
min_days: int
looks: int = 1
def ready_to_analyse(plan: TestPlan, n_per_arm_now: int, days_run: int) -> bool:
"""True only once the planned sample and duration are both reached."""
return n_per_arm_now >= plan.n_per_arm and days_run >= plan.min_days

exercises.prompt: Write `peeking_false_positive_rate(rng, n_sims, n_per_look, looks, rate, z_crit=1.959964) -> float`. It simulates `n_sims` A/A tests where both arms convert at `rate`. Each arm gets `n_per_look` new users per look. At each look, run a pooled two-proportion z-test on the cumulative data. Return the share of simulations where `|z| > z_crit` at **any** look. Treat a zero standard error as z = 0. Use only the `rng` passed in.
exercises.prompt_html: Write peeking_false_positive_rate(rng, n_sims, n_per_look, looks, rate, z_crit=1.959964) -> float. It simulates n_sims A/A tests where both arms convert at rate. Each arm gets n_per_look new users per look. At each look, run a pooled two-proportion z-test on the cumulative data. Return the share of simulations where |z| > z_crit at any look. Treat a zero standard error as z = 0. Use only the rng passed in.
exercises.solution:
import numpy as np


def peeking_false_positive_rate(
    rng: np.random.Generator,
    n_sims: int,
    n_per_look: int,
    looks: int,
    rate: float,
    z_crit: float = 1.959964,
) -> float:
    """Share of A/A simulations declared significant at any of the looks.

    Args:
        rng: Seeded generator.
        n_sims: Number of simulated tests.
        n_per_look: New users per arm between looks.
        looks: Number of analyses.
        rate: True conversion rate in both arms.
        z_crit: Two-sided threshold for each look.

    Returns:
        The false positive rate across simulations.
    """
    total = looks * n_per_look
    a = (rng.random((n_sims, total)) < rate).cumsum(axis=1)
    b = (rng.random((n_sims, total)) < rate).cumsum(axis=1)
    idx = np.arange(1, looks + 1) * n_per_look - 1
    n = idx + 1
    xa, xb = a[:, idx], b[:, idx]
    pooled = (xa + xb) / (2 * n)
    se = np.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * 2 / n)
    diff = (xb - xa) / n
    z = np.divide(diff, se, out=np.zeros_like(diff), where=se > 0)
    return float((np.abs(z) > z_crit).any(axis=1).mean())

def peeking_false_positive_rate(
rng: np.random.Generator,
n_sims: int,
n_per_look: int,
looks: int,
rate: float,
z_crit: float = 1.959964,
) -> float:
"""Share of A/A simulations declared significant at any of the looks.
Args:
rng: Seeded generator.
n_sims: Number of simulated tests.
n_per_look: New users per arm between looks.
looks: Number of analyses.
rate: True conversion rate in both arms.
z_crit: Two-sided threshold for each look.
Returns:
The false positive rate across simulations.
"""
total = looks * n_per_look
a = (rng.random((n_sims, total)) < rate).cumsum(axis=1)
b = (rng.random((n_sims, total)) < rate).cumsum(axis=1)
idx = np.arange(1, looks + 1) * n_per_look - 1
n = idx + 1
xa, xb = a[:, idx], b[:, idx]
pooled = (xa + xb) / (2 * n)
se = np.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * 2 / n)
diff = (xb - xa) / n
z = np.divide(diff, se, out=np.zeros_like(diff), where=se > 0)
return float((np.abs(z) > z_crit).any(axis=1).mean())

title: Peeking, novelty and other ways tests mislead
why_html: A growth team ran 30 tests a quarter, checked each daily, and shipped any variant that reached p < 0.05. Their dashboard showed 11 winners, with a combined forecast lift of 9% in sign-ups. Sign-ups over the quarter were flat. With daily peeking over three-week tests, the false positive rate per test was far above 5%, and most of the winners were noise.
